subject: thiel
summary: Co-founder of PayPal and Palantir and Facebook's first outside investor. chapters.title: Frankfurt, Foster City and Stanford
chapters.dek: A philosophy student who built a conservative newspaper and a first book around campus politics.
chapters.body:
Thiel was born in Frankfurt am Main on October 11, 1967 [[wikidata]]. His family moved to the United States when he was an infant, lived in Cleveland, spent several years in South West Africa (now Namibia), and settled in Foster City, California, in 1977 [[wikipedia]].

He studied philosophy at Stanford, graduating in 1989. In 1987 he co-founded The Stanford Review, a student paper set up to challenge what its founders saw as political conformity on campus, and was its first editor-in-chief [[wikipedia, palantir-board]]. The argument became his first book, The Diversity Myth (1995), written with David Sacks, which criticised Stanford's multicultural curriculum [[independent-diversity-myth]].

After Stanford Law School (JD, 1992) he clerked for Judge J. L. Edmondson of the Eleventh Circuit, practised securities law at Sullivan & Cromwell and traded derivatives at Credit Suisse, then returned to California in 1996 to start Thiel Capital Management [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: PayPal and the first fortune
chapters.dek: A payments start-up, a merger with Elon Musk's company, and a $1.5 billion sale.
chapters.body:
In 1998 Thiel co-founded Confinity, whose payments product, PayPal, launched the following year [[palantir-board, wikipedia]]. Confinity merged with Elon Musk's X.com in 2000, and Thiel served as PayPal's chief executive, president and chairman from 2000 until its sale [[palantir-board]].

PayPal went public on February 15, 2002. That October eBay bought it for $1.5 billion, which left Thiel's stake of roughly 3.7 percent worth about $55 million [[wikipedia]].

Several early PayPal staff, among them Musk and Sacks, went on to found or fund major technology companies, a group later nicknamed the "PayPal Mafia" [[wikipedia]]. Both later became political figures in their own right.

chapters.title: Palantir, Facebook and Founders Fund
chapters.dek: The companies and funds that made him a billionaire, and employed two future Senate candidates.
chapters.body:
Thiel incorporated Palantir in May 2003 with a small group of co-founders including Joe Lonsdale, and has chaired its board since [[palantir-board, lonsdale-8vc, wikipedia]].

In August 2004 he paid $500,000 for 10.2 percent of Facebook, the company's first outside investment [[wikipedia]]. He sat on its board, which became Meta Platforms' board in 2021, until 2022 [[palantir-board, fortune-meta-2022]]. After Facebook's 2012 IPO he sold nearly all his remaining shares, for more than $1 billion in total [[wikipedia]].

He has been a partner at Founders Fund since 2005 [[palantir-board, founders-fund-team]]. He also started Clarium Capital, a macro hedge fund, after the PayPal sale, co-founded Valar Ventures in 2010 and Mithril Capital in 2012, and has been president of Thiel Capital since 2011 [[wikipedia, palantir-board]]. In 2010 his foundation launched the Thiel Fellowship, which pays people under 20 $100,000 to leave or skip college and build something [[venturebeat-fellowship]].

Two of these firms later supplied Republican Senate candidates. JD Vance worked at Mithril before starting his own fund, Narya Capital, in 2019. Blake Masters, Thiel's co-author on Zero to One, was chief operating officer of Thiel Capital and president of the Thiel Foundation [[wikipedia-narya, wikipedia-masters]].

chapters.title: A libertarian against democracy
chapters.dek: The 2009 essay that defined his politics, and the case for monopoly.
chapters.body:
Thiel still used the libertarian label in 2009, but the essay that made his politics widely discussed qualified it sharply. In "The Education of a Libertarian," published by Cato Unbound that April, he wrote:

> I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible. [[cato-2009]]

He argued that the growth of welfare spending and the extension of the vote to women since 1920 had made "capitalist democracy" an oxymoron. After the line drew wide criticism, he added a note saying he did not think "any class of people should be disenfranchised," but had "little hope that voting will make things better" [[cato-2009]]. His alternative was technological: cyberspace, outer space and seasteading as frontiers beyond the reach of existing politics.

A second argument runs through his business writing: that lasting companies escape competition rather than win it. It is the core of Zero to One (2014), which grew out of Blake Masters's notes on a course Thiel taught at Stanford in 2012 [[techcrunch-zero-to-one]], and of a Wall Street Journal essay adapted from the book, which argued that capitalism and competition are opposites [[wsj-2014]].

chapters.title: From Ron Paul to Donald Trump
chapters.dek: A selective donor who backed Trump early in 2016, then pulled back.
chapters.body:
FEC filings record Thiel's federal giving from 2000, mostly to Republican candidates and party committees, including Ron Paul's House campaigns [[fec-sa-thiel]]. In the 2012 cycle he gave $2.6 million to Endorse Liberty, a super PAC supporting Paul's presidential bid [[fec-sa-thiel, wikipedia]].

In 2016 he was one of very few prominent technology figures to back Donald Trump. He was a Trump delegate and, on July 21, spoke at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland, where he became the first convention speaker to say he was gay [[wikipedia, abc-rnc-2016]]:

> I am proud to be gay. I am proud to be a Republican. But most of all I am proud to be an American. [[fortune-rnc-2016]]

The same speech said "fake culture wars only distract us from our economic decline," and contrasted the Cold War with a debate over "who gets to use which bathroom" [[fortune-rnc-2016]]. In October he gave $1 million to Make America Number 1, a pro-Trump super PAC, and $250,000 to the Trump Victory joint fundraising committee [[fec-sa-thiel]]. After the election he was named to the executive committee of Trump's transition [[p2016-transition, fortune-transition-2016]].

He did not repeat the role. FEC records show no comparable gifts to Trump's 2020 campaign, and in April 2023 Reuters reported that he had told associates he would fund no candidates in 2024, because he thought the party was too focused on cultural issues [[fec-sa-thiel, reuters-2023]]. His filings since then show gifts to party committees and a $1.5 million contribution to Club for Growth Action in February 2026 [[fec-sa-thiel]].

chapters.title: Vance, Masters and the 2022 Senate races
chapters.dek: $35 million to two super PACs, each built around a former employee.
chapters.body:
The 2022 Senate primaries were Thiel's largest political outlay. In March and April 2021 he gave $10 million each to two new super PACs, Protect Ohio Values PAC and Saving Arizona PAC. By October 2022 his contributions had reached $15 million to the Ohio committee and $20 million to the Arizona one [[fec-sa-thiel]].

Each committee spent mainly on one candidate, both former Thiel employees. Protect Ohio Values reported $14.7 million in independent expenditures supporting JD Vance; Saving Arizona reported $13.0 million supporting Blake Masters, and more against his primary and general-election opponents [[fec-ie-2022]]. Federal law limited an individual's direct gifts to a candidate's campaign to $2,900 per election that cycle, so nearly all of this money moved through the super PACs rather than the campaigns.

In February 2022 Thiel announced he would leave Meta's board to concentrate on the midterms [[fortune-meta-2022]]. Vance won in Ohio; Masters won his primary and lost to Senator Mark Kelly in November [[reuters-2023]].

In July 2024 Trump chose Vance as his running mate. Reporting at the time traced the technology investors, Thiel among them, who had backed Vance's career [[wapo-2024]]. Vance took office as vice president in January 2025 [[whitehouse-vance]].

chapters.title: The Gawker case
chapters.dek: Secret litigation funding that ended a publisher.
chapters.body:
In 2007 Gawker Media's Valleywag blog published a post headlined "Peter Thiel is totally gay, people" [[wikipedia]]. Thiel later secretly paid for lawsuits against the company, including former wrestler Terry Bollea's (Hulk Hogan's) suit over a sex tape Gawker had published in 2012 [[cnbc-forbes-2016, nyt-sorkin-2016]]. In March 2016 a Florida jury awarded Bollea $140 million [[cnbc-forbes-2016]].

Forbes revealed Thiel's role on May 24, 2016. The next day he confirmed it to The New York Times, which reported that he had spent about $10 million on the litigation [[nyt-sorkin-2016, wikipedia]]:

> It's less about revenge and more about specific deterrence. [[nyt-sorkin-2016]]

Gawker Media filed for bankruptcy in June and in November settled with Bollea for $31 million [[cnn-settlement-2016]]. In an August op-ed Thiel presented the case as a defence of private individuals, arguing that journalism does not require indiscriminate access to people's sex lives [[nyt-oped-2016]]. Reporters and First Amendment specialists warned that it showed how a wealthy patron could use litigation to silence critics [[techcrunch-gawker-2016]].

chapters.title: Girard, Christianity and the Antichrist
chapters.dek: A theology of technology, and lately of catastrophe.
chapters.body:
Thiel describes himself as a Christian. His account of faith draws on René Girard, the French literary theorist he encountered at Stanford, whose theory of imitation, rivalry and scapegoating he cites as a lasting influence [[america-2014, wikipedia]]. In a 2014 interview he argued that Christianity is compatible with technological progress and can motivate it [[america-2014]].

More recently his religious arguments have turned to the end times. In a June 2025 interview with Ross Douthat he described an Antichrist who might come to power promising peace and safety, through global governance that halts science and technology [[douthat-2025]]. That September and October he gave four off-the-record lectures on the Antichrist at San Francisco's Commonwealth Club, organized by the ACTS 17 Collective. They were not recorded, so public accounts of them come from attendees [[sfstandard-2025]].
